nameStory: Rock polypody gets its name from its favorite hangout spot – rocky crevices and cliff faces where it seems to grow right out of stone. The word 'polypody' comes from Greek meaning 'many feet,' referring to the branching underground stems that spread like little feet across rock surfaces.
description: Rock polypody is a charming small evergreen fern that specializes in making its home on rocks and boulders. This tough little plant forms dense mats of leathery, finger-like fronds that stay green all year round. Each frond is typically hand-sized, growing in a simple once-divided pattern that looks like a green feather with rounded lobes along each side.

idTips.label: Fronds
idTips.description: Leathery, evergreen fronds with a simple once-divided pattern featuring rounded lobes that feel thick and waxy to the touch, like leather that's been well-oiled

idTips.label: Sori
idTips.description: Round, golden-brown dots arranged in neat rows on the underside of fertile fronds, looking like tiny copper pennies scattered across the surface

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms dense spreading mats by creeping underground stems, with fronds emerging individually rather than in clusters or crowns

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Almost always found growing directly on rock surfaces, especially in cracks and crevices where a thin layer of soil has accumulated

idTips.label: Stipe
idTips.description: Short, smooth stems that feel firm and are often hidden beneath the spreading fronds, typically much shorter than the frond blade itself

habitat: Rock polypody thrives on exposed rock faces, cliff ledges, and boulder fields throughout New England's mountains and hills. Look for it in the thin soil that collects in rock crevices, especially on north-facing slopes where moisture lingers longer. It's particularly common on granite outcrops and stone walls in forested areas.

seasonality.spring: New fiddleheads emerge from rock crevices as small, tightly coiled spirals covered in rusty scales. The existing evergreen fronds from last year will still be prominently displayed.
seasonality.summer: Fronds reach full size and develop their characteristic leathery texture. Spore-bearing sori appear as golden dots on the undersides of mature fronds.
seasonality.fall: Sori mature and release spores, turning from golden to brown. The evergreen fronds remain vibrant and green as other vegetation begins to fade.
seasonality.winter: One of the few ferns that stays bright green through snow and ice, making it easy to spot against bare rock faces and winter landscapes.

funFact: Rock polypody is like nature's air conditioning system – it can lose up to 75% of its water content during dry spells and appear completely dead, then spring back to life within hours of the next rainfall, earning it the nickname 'resurrection fern' in some regions.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with Christmas fern, but Christmas fern grows in soil rather than on rocks and has much more pointed, holly-like leaflets. Remember: polypody = rock lover with rounded lobes, Christmas fern = soil dweller with sharp points.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this tough little rock-dweller with the tropical 'resurrection fern' (Pleopeltis polypodioides) that grows on tree bark in the South – they're different species that just happen to share the same amazing drought-survival trick.
compareHints: Rock polypody differs from its close relative, Appalachian rockcap fern, mainly through microscopic spore characteristics that require expert examination. In the field, they're nearly impossible to distinguish reliably, and many botanists consider them part of a species complex that may represent varieties of the same plant rather than separate species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Appalachian rockcap fern is virtually identical to rock polypody in appearance, but tends to grow in slightly more sheltered, cooler spots on rock faces.
